about.story.title: Interesting before pretty.
about.story.p1: Petals & Predators started with a single Venus flytrap on a kitchen windowsill — and the small shock of watching it actually catch a fly. That curiosity grew into a greenhouse, and the greenhouse grew into a boutique built around two things that rarely share a shelf: carnivorous plants and flowers with real character.
about.story.p2: We are a small team of growers who believe a plant should be interesting before it is pretty. Some of ours bite. Others bloom. All of them are chosen because they bring something alive and a little unexpected into a room.
about.story.p3: Every specimen is grown in-house, packed by hand, and shipped with the care it needs to arrive thriving. If it does not, we make it right — that part is a promise, not a slogan.
about.story.image-alt: Editorial illustration of a carnivorous plant in the greenhouse

about.grow.value-1.title: Hand-pollinated

about.grow.value-2.title: Peat-based mixes
about.grow.value-2.body: We grow in nutrient-poor, peat-based substrate mixed to each species, never regular potting soil that burns their roots.
about.grow.value-3.title: Ventilated boxes
about.grow.value-3.body: Plants travel in ventilated boxes with a moisture collar, so they arrive hydrated, upright, and ready to grow.

contact.care.title: No green thumb needed.
contact.care.body: A few habits keep carnivorous plants and blooms thriving. Every order also ships with a printed guide in the box.
contact.care.tip-1.title: Light
contact.care.tip-1.body: Bright, indirect light for most species. Carnivorous plants love a sunny windowsill — just avoid harsh midday sun.
contact.care.tip-2.title: Water
contact.care.tip-2.body: Use rainwater or distilled water for carnivorous plants. Keep the soil damp, never bone-dry, and skip tap water when you can.
contact.care.tip-3.title: Substrate
contact.care.tip-3.body: We grow in peat-based, nutrient-poor mixes. Repot with the same blend — regular potting soil burns their roots.
contact.care.tip-4.title: Feeding
contact.care.tip-4.body: Let them hunt. Indoors they usually catch enough on their own, so resist the urge to feed them by hand.
